analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to give or accept gifts rewarding state and local officials' official actions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with three Democratic cosponsors, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under existing federal law, bribing a state or local official is a crime, but a thank-you gift given after the official act is not. This bill would add gratuities to the federal bribery statute for state, local, and tribal officials involved in government business worth $5,000 or more, with fines and up to two years in prison. It was introduced late in the 118th Congress and died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on honest state and local government. If a city awards a contract or a county regulates a business, the people affected would know the decision-maker could not legally be rewarded with gifts afterward by the party that won. Public officials who follow the rules also benefit, because the bill sets a clear bright line separating legitimate gifts from secret rewards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents who depend on honest local government

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new prohibition on gratuities to federal bribery law for state, local, and tribal officials, covering gifts given to reward official actions involving $5,000 or more in government business, punishable by up to two years in prison [S2].
Covers both sides of the exchange: officials who solicit, demand, or accept a reward, and anyone who gives, offers, or agrees to give one [S2].
Preserves an existing exception for legitimate salary, wages, and fees paid for proper official work, so ordinary compensation is not criminalized [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and contractors who win state, local, or tribal government deals worth $5,000 or more would lose the ability to give officials post-decision gifts or rewards, and would face federal criminal exposure for doing so. State, local, and tribal officials would face federal charges for accepting or soliciting such rewards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Contractors and officials in gift-for-deal exchanges

drawbacks.text: The prohibition reaches any reward connected to government business of $5,000 or more, which could sweep in gifts or payments with ambiguous motives and raise fair-notice questions for people who did not intend a corrupt bargain [S2].

Existing law already criminalizes bribes agreed to before an official act, so the bill's main effect is extending criminal liability to after-the-fact rewards, a line the courts drew narrowly in 2024; critics argue gratitude gifts are hard to distinguish from lawful thanks, while supporters argue that is exactly the loophole that rewards officials after the fact [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but narrow: it closes a gap that lets officials be rewarded after their decisions instead of before them. The cost is a new federal criminal exposure for a wide range of gift-giving around government deals, mitigated by the two-year penalty cap and the carve-out for legitimate pay and fees. On balance it strengthens anti-corruption enforcement at modest risk, but it received no committee work, so no one had to defend or refine the design in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, joined by Senators Warren, Whitehouse, and Welch [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the bill sat in committee with no markup, hearing, or floor vote listed before the 118th Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contractors and officials who benefit from the current rule that post-decision gifts are not a federal crime, and a Judiciary Committee that never had to take a position on closing that gap. Ordinary residents of state and local jurisdictions gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contractors and officials facing no new gift limits

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; no further action followed.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it attracted.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor joined, though there is no record of any party blocking it because the committee never acted.

industries.industry: Businesses seeking state, local, and tribal government contracts
industries.note: The bill makes it a federal crime to give or promise gifts rewarding officials on government deals worth $5,000 or more. These companies' interest in keeping after-the-fact rewards legal runs against residents who want contracting decisions made on the merits.

industries.industry: State, local, and tribal public officials
industries.note: Officials who solicit or accept gifts rewarding their official actions would face up to two years in prison. Their interest in the current gift rules runs against the public's interest in untainted decisions.
